soil-found-077.title: Soil: rock, water, air and life in one mixture
soil-found-077.text: A single gram of soil can hold billions of organisms from thousands of species, most of them microbes that no one has yet explored. Soil is a natural mixture of minerals, {{ref:soil-bio-114}}, gases, water and organisms that together support the life of plants and soil creatures. All of Earth's soil, taken together, forms one layer with a name of its own, the subject of {{ref:soil-found-084}}. Soil is a three-state system. A solid framework of minerals and dead plant and animal material is laced with pores. Those pores hold gases, the soil atmosphere, and water carrying dissolved substances, the soil solution. Much of a soil is empty space. A dry sample of most soils weighs 1.1 to 1.6 grams per cubic centimeter, yet the particles themselves weigh 2.6 to 2.7. Soil is made by climate, relief, organisms and the rock or sediment beneath acting together over time, and it never stops developing. It is also young. Little of it is older than the Pleistocene and none is older than the Cenozoic, though fossilized soils survive from as far back as the Archean. Soil has four important functions. It grows plants, stores and purifies water, modifies Earth's atmosphere and houses soil organisms. It is a large reservoir of carbon, and possibly one of the most sensitive to human disturbance and climate change. Soil ecologists regard it as an ecosystem in its own right. Some scientific definitions keep the word dirt for soil that has been moved out of place.

soil-found-090.title: Soil science: one resource, many disciplines
soil-found-090.text: Engineers, agronomists, chemists, geologists, ecologists, microbiologists, archaeologists and planners all add to what is known about soils. Soil science gathers that knowledge into the study of soil as a natural resource. It asks how soil forms and how it is classified and mapped. It measures soil's physical, chemical, biological and fertility properties, and asks how they bear on its use and management. The field has two main historical branches. {{ref:soil-found-095}} studies soil in its natural setting. {{ref:soil-found-097}} studies soil in relation to the uses that depend on it. Both draw on the physics, chemistry and biology of soil. Soil occupies {{ref:soil-found-084}}, one of the spheres the geosciences use to organize the Earth. Climate change, greenhouse gases and carbon sequestration now drive much new research, along with interest in biodiversity and in past cultures. Soil scientists also worry about preserving soil and farmland as population and food consumption grow and more land is degraded. Mapping, which classifies the soils of an area and geo-encodes them, increasingly relies on digital methods and remote sensing. In 1998 a new international system, {{ref:soil-class-016}}, replaced the older one from the FAO. Its current 4th edition dates from 2022.

soil-found-084.title: Where four spheres meet: the pedosphere
soil-found-084.text: Soil forms only where four of Earth's great systems touch. The pedosphere is the outermost layer of Earth's crust, made of soil, where soil forms and wears away by erosion. It lies at the meeting point of the lithosphere, the rocky shell, with the atmosphere, the hydrosphere of Earth's waters and the biosphere of living things. Soil develops only where all four interact. The pedosphere is the foundation of every ecosystem on land, and it passes chemical and biogeochemical flows into and out of the other spheres. It sits within a wider interface that runs from vegetation through aquifers and loose material down into solid rock, described in {{ref:soil-found-115}}. Soil begins to form as minerals over solid rock break down, chemically or physically. It can start without life, but biological reactions speed it up greatly. Chemical attack on silicon-bearing minerals dominates the work. Acids from {{ref:soil-found-085}} help, and so does carbonic acid from the atmosphere. The rock below sets the starting conditions, and few rock types locally enrich scarce elements such as phosphorus and nitrogen. Over time the soil's bulk chemistry drifts away from the rock's. It comes to reflect the reactions taking place in the soil itself.

soil-found-095.title: Pedology: reading how a soil came to be
soil-found-095.text: Every soil has a life story, and pedology sets out to read it. Pedology is the branch of soil science that studies how soils form and evolve, and builds frameworks for describing them, often where they lie in nature. Pedologists observe a soil's form, where soils occur and how they fit into wider settings of time and space. From those observations come classifications, soil maps and theories. As a soil forms, it slowly deepens and develops characteristic layers, approaching a steady state. Fallou conceived pedology in the 19th century as a fundamental science, separate from agrology, the applied forerunner of {{ref:soil-found-097}}. For a long time agronomists saw soil as a static production medium, while pedologists studied its ties to landscape history. The two approaches are now integrated. One sub-discipline characterizes and maps soils with numbers. Another, soil geomorphology, links landform processes with the way soils form.

soil-found-097.title: Edaphology: what soil does for living things
soil-found-097.text: Long before the word existed, Xenophon and Cato were practicing edaphology. Cato recommended working the soil, rotating crops and growing legumes to build soil nitrogen. He also devised the first soil capability classification for crops. Edaphology is the branch of soil science concerned with how soils influence living things, especially plants. Alongside pedology, it is one of the field's two main divisions. It covers how soil shapes people's use of land for plant growth and other purposes. Its general subfields deal with farming, called agrology in some regions, and with the environment. The environmental side ranges from septic fields, wastewater and storm runoff to controlling erosion, contamination and cleanup, restoring wetlands and managing nutrients. At first the two branches were poorly distinguished. Russian soil scientists used edaphology as a synonym for pedology, and Spanish ones preferred the term. In the 20th century edaphology was driven out of a pedology-centered science. It is now recognized as a necessary branch, complementary to pedology.

soil-found-078.title: Half solid, half empty: what a soil is made of
soil-found-078.text: Half of a typical soil is not solid at all. About 50% of its volume is solids, 45% mineral grains and 5% material from living things, alive or dead. The other 50% is pores, half filled with water and half with gas. Soil composition describes these proportions. In the short term the mineral and organic shares stay constant, while water and gas trade places. A rise in one is balanced by a fall in the other. Pore space matters because air and water must enter and move through it, and both are critical for soil life. Squeezing a soil, especially under heavy machinery, shrinks its pores and keeps air and water from roots and organisms. Mineral particles, interacting with the organic share, water and gases, clump together into crumbs. Where these crumbs can be identified, the soil is said to be developed. Most nutrients are held by the finest particles of clay and organic material. They cling to clay surfaces, sit bound inside clay minerals, or are locked in living organisms and in long-decayed organic remains. Apart from nitrogen fixed from the atmosphere, most plant nutrients first came from the minerals of the rock or sediment the soil formed from. Living things shape a soil most strongly near the surface. With depth, geochemical influences take over.

soil-found-081.title: From food to foundations: how people use soil
soil-found-081.text: Soil resources produce 98.8% of the food humans consume. In farming, soil anchors plants and is their primary nutrient base. The kind of soil and the moisture available decide which plants can be grown. Yet soil is not strictly essential. Systems that grow plants in water or mist, with no soil at all, show as much. Soil is also the foundation for most construction and the basis of many building materials. Surface mining, road building and dam construction move massive volumes of it. Waste treatment relies on soil too. Septic drain fields and wastewater spread on land use soil processes that need oxygen, and landfills use soil as daily cover. Water percolating down to become groundwater is filtered on the way, losing pesticides, hydrocarbons, heavy metals and excess nutrients. Organic soils are a significant fuel and horticultural resource, and drained peatlands are farmed in Nordic countries. Animals and humans even eat soil-like substances, a habit called geophagy. Some monkeys eat soil with their leaves to ease tannin toxicity.

soil-found-082.title: Mending poor soils with clay, sand and char
soil-found-082.text: In Thai field trials, a single dose of clay raised yields on low-clay soils by an average of 73%. The trials added a swelling clay once, at 200 kilograms per rai, or 1,300 kg/ha. Soil reclamation improves degraded or badly balanced soils by adding materials such as clay, gypsum, sand, plant and animal remains or {{ref:soil-fert-050}}. Soils too high in clay or salts can be balanced with gypsum and washed river sand. Sandy, nutrient-poor soils benefit from compost or ramial chipped wood. Charred material, modeled on fertile Amazonian Dark Earths, is used to improve nutrient-poor tropical soils. Uncontrolled use of charred wastes, though, may endanger soil life and human health.

soil-found-091.title: Dokuchaev's idea: soil as a natural body with a history
soil-found-091.text: As late as 1914, an encyclopedia defined soil as forms of earth made as rocks weather. That was the old view. Soil was a product of chemical changes in rock, a dead substrate from which plants draw their nutrients. Fallou and Dokuchaev are both credited among the first to treat soil as something distinct from geology and from crop production. Fallou came first, but Dokuchaev's work proved more significant. He saw soil as a natural body with its own genesis and history, distinct from the solid rock beneath it. Rock becomes soil, he held, under the action of climate, vegetation, country, relief and age. In the 20th century the concept became one of earthy material altered by living processes. It is still being refined to take in energy moving within soil. Nikiforoff's 1959 definition fits this modern understanding: soil is the 'excited skin of the sub aerial part of the Earth's crust'.

soil-env-181.title: The many jobs a soil does
soil-env-181.text: About 50% of people live in houses built from soil. Shelter is one of soil's functions, the general capabilities that matter for farming, the environment, nature protection, landscape architecture and city life. To grow food and biomass, soil stores and supplies nutrients and holds water in its pores. It swaps carbon dioxide for fresh oxygen around roots and moderates temperature. It is a habitat and gene reserve for many organisms, and it turns dead plants and animals into simple mineral forms that other life can use. Food reflects the soil it grew in, so soil shapes human health. Roads and buildings depend on how much weight soil bears, how far it compresses and how well it holds together. Productive soil is limited in area. As cropping, forestry and cities spread, digging it out as a raw material needs control. Soil is also cultural heritage. It gives a sense of place, preserves artifacts of the past and has guided where people settle.

soil-env-174.title: Soil health: treating the ground as a living system
soil-env-174.text: Some microbiologists believe that 80% of a soil's nutrient functions are essentially controlled by microbes. That view sits at the heart of soil health, the state of a soil meeting its range of ecosystem functions as suits its environment. The underlying principle is that soil is a living, dynamic, ever-changing environment. It is not the inert growing medium that intensive farming tends to assume. Put simply, health arises from favorable interactions among all of a soil's parts, living and non-living, from microbes to plants and animals. The term spans sustaining plant and animal productivity, enhancing biodiversity, maintaining water and air quality, and supporting human health and habitation. Soils highly fertile for crops are also biologically lively. Temperate grassland soils hold 1–2 t/ha of bacterial biomass and 2–5 t/ha of fungal biomass. By analogy with human health, a healthy soil is in biological, chemical and physical well-being. It is not degraded, it resists degradation, and it keeps cycling nutrients, carbon and water. Soil health depends on the variety of life in the soil. Keeping protective living covers on the soil and adding natural, carbon-containing amendments improve it. Inorganic fertilizers need not harm it, if they are not used in excess and the extra plant growth returns more carbon-containing residues. The idea remains debated. A soil can be healthy for its ecosystem without directly serving crop production, so scientists still disagree on how to define and measure soil health.

soil-env-179.title: Soil quality, the standard no one has fixed
soil-env-179.text: Water and air have established quality standards. Soil does not, because its quality is difficult to define or quantify. Soil quality is the condition of a soil judged by its capacity to perform ecosystem services for human and non-human life. It reflects how well a soil maintains biodiversity and productivity, partitions the flow of water and dissolved substances, filters and buffers, cycles nutrients and supports plants and structures. Management has a major impact. Planting cover crops, for example, raises soil quality by adding plant remains over time. Soil organisms contribute in countless ways, and the amount and diversity of soil life appears proportional to soil quality. Fungi that partner with plant roots help their hosts establish on degraded soil and improve its quality and health.

soil-found-096.title: The ground rules pedologists use to explain soils
soil-found-096.text: Much of the world's shale began as soil. Soils are natural clay factories, and their clay, eroded into ocean basins, later hardened into rock. Pedologists explain how soils form with a set of working principles. The first is that external factors drive soil-forming processes and create soil patterns. Five major factors dominate: climate, organisms, relief, the rock or sediment beneath, and time. Complexity is more common than simplicity, and today's soils carry imprints of past processes that may be hard to observe. Those processes create and destroy order within a soil, often at once, and its layers record the balance. Uniformitarianism, the idea that present processes also ran in the past, applies too: they have worked since organisms first appeared on land. Few soils are geologically old. Most date no further back than the Pleistocene. Knowing soil genesis aids classification, mapping and management. Yet classifications cannot rest on genesis alone, since its processes are seldom observed and change over time.

soil-found-093.title: What soil scientists actually do
soil-found-093.text: Almost every area of the United States has had its soils surveyed and published, with tables on how their properties support or limit different uses. Mapping soils is the traditional work of soil scientists. Increasingly, they also take on land and environmental problems across disciplines. They protect environmentally critical areas and valuable habitats, manage land for productivity and remediate damaged land. Some applications are less obvious: dating past activity at a site, reading archaeological layers, vitrifying radioactive waste and using soil microbes to degrade contaminants. The concept of {{ref:soil-found-115}} frames research across soil, rock, air, water and living resources at Earth's surface.

soil-found-092.title: Red, hot, fat or sandy: soils by their folk names
soil-found-092.text: The earliest known scheme for sorting soils comes from China. The Yu Gong, from the 5th century BCE, sorted soil into three categories and nine classes by color, grain and water. Vernacular classifications are folk systems that give soils unique names or name them by obvious traits such as red, hot, fat or sandy. They judge soils by appearance, performance and the plants growing on them. A familiar example contrasts heavy, clayey soils with light, sandy ones. Light soils are easier to cultivate and resist compaction by trampling cattle, but they erode more easily. Despite the name, they are not lighter or more porous than heavy soils.

soil-found-086.title: What the sky drops into the soil
soil-found-086.text: After water itself, nitrogen is the most abundant ingredient of rain. The reason is that water vapor uses tiny airborne particles, called aerosols, to form droplets. Rain is one of three main inputs the pedosphere receives from the air. The others are wind-blown sediment and gases diffusing in. Wind carries aerosols, pollen and dust into soils, a process called eolian sedimentation. Gases move both ways. Carbon dioxide from roots and microbes keeps the bicarbonate in soil water far above balance with the air. Together with dissolved metals, this makes the soil more acid. Gases escape back to the air from dissolving carbonates, decay, chemical reactions and microbial photosynthesis.

soil-found-087.title: Forest soils, leached into sharp bands
soil-found-087.text: In a forest, more water falls as rain and snow than evaporates or passes back out through plants. The surplus percolates down through the soil layers. Forest soils form in these conditions and are usually well developed, with thick layers of well-decayed organic remains. Slow decay releases large amounts of a soluble organic acid, which greatly enhances the chemical breakdown of minerals. Percolating water and this breakdown carry magnesium, iron and aluminum downward, a process called podzolization. The result is marked contrasts in color and chemistry between layers. Forest soils can also build a thick sponge of stored carbon.

soil-found-089.title: Grassland and desert soils, shaped by drought
soil-found-089.text: Drought writes itself into a soil. Grassland and desert soils form where rain and snow equal or fall short of the water lost to evaporation and plants. Little water and few organic acids percolate downward. So the washing out of dissolved substances slows, along with chemical breakdown of minerals and soil development itself. Evaporation builds up calcium in the upper profile, where it clumps clay and dissolved organic acids together. Lower down, calcium settles out as a hard layer of calcite. In deserts a layer of gypsum and halite may lie beneath it. Where rain and washing out increase, the clay-richest layer sits deeper.

soil-found-085.title: Lichens, microbes and the first bite into bare rock
soil-found-085.text: Bare rock starts becoming soil when living things attack it with acid. The first colonizers, such as lichens, mosses and microbes, begin the work. Lichens and other microorganisms, including cyanobacteria, green algae, fungi and bacteria, secrete oxalic acid. Lichens have long been seen as the pioneers of soil. Seed-bearing plants can colonize faster, but lichens tolerate harsher conditions and dominate in alpine regions. Organic acids from roots and decay, such as citric, phenolic, humic and fulvic acids, speed chemical breakdown by gripping metal atoms and pulling them from minerals. As the soil thickens, earthworms, burrowing mammals and large animals above ground go on altering its chemistry and fertility.

soil-found-088.title: Why tropical forest soils turn rusty red
soil-found-088.text: No other environment gets as much sunlight and rain over such long growing seasons as the tropical forest. Its plants produce as much as 800 grams of carbon per square meter per year, or 8 tons per hectare. Heat and abundant water speed the chemical breakdown of minerals. Decay is fast too, leaving less organic acid to wash metals downward. So unlike temperate {{ref:soil-found-087}}, tropical forest soils show little or no podzolization and lack marked contrasts between layers. Mobile magnesium, iron and aluminum instead settle out as oxides, giving the soil a rusty red color.

soil-found-099.title: How industrial farming changed soil and crop
soil-found-099.text: Heavy metals from mechanized production have built up in soils, and they have turned up in crops as well. Industrialization has changed how soils interact with plants, the core concern of {{ref:soil-found-097}}. Greater use of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides has decreased the nutrients soils make available. Growing a single crop over and over lowers biodiversity. That reduces soil nutrients further and deepens dependence on chemical fertilizer. Intensive plowing and digging disturb the soil microbes that help keep soil moist and its air circulating.

soil-found-098.title: Van Helmont's willow and a pot of soil
soil-found-098.text: For five years Jan Baptist van Helmont (1577–1644) grew a willow tree in a pot of soil, supplying nothing but rainwater. At the end, the tree had gained more weight than the soil had lost. Van Helmont concluded that the willow was made of water. He was only partly correct, but the experiment reignited interest in edaphology, the study of how soils shape plant life.

soil-found-115.title: The critical zone, from living soil down to bedrock
soil-found-115.text: Nearly all life on land depends on a zone that ends deep in solid rock, where life and water stop significantly changing the rock's chemistry. Earth's critical zone is the near-surface environment where rock, soil, water, air and living organisms interact. Together they regulate habitats and the availability of life-sustaining resources. The zone runs through the pedosphere, the unsaturated ground below it and the saturated groundwater zone. In practice it essentially equates to the pedosphere. Its uppermost, biota-rich layer is called the biomantle. Its processes govern the exchanges of mass and energy behind biomass production, chemical cycling and water storage. Critical Zone science integrates landscape evolution, rock breakdown, hydrology, geochemistry and ecology, across scales of space and time and human influence. Tsakalotos coined the term in chemistry in 1909. Gail Ashley applied it in 1998 to the connection of vegetation to soil and weathered materials. It is studied at Critical Zone Observatories, for which the US National Science Foundation sought proposals in 2006.

soil-found-080.title: Can lifeless ground be called soil?
soil-found-080.text: Is the ground on Mars soil? Only part of the scientific community accepts the word for the surface material of the Moon and Mars. The question belongs to an unsettled debate over where soil ends and other loose surface material begins. One classic definition says soil has formed once dead plant and animal material accumulates and fine particles washed down from above build a distinct lower layer. That definition is somewhat arbitrary. Mixtures of mineral grains and decayed organic remains support biological and farming activity before such a layer forms. Twentieth-century thinking cast soil as earthy material altered by living processes. On that view, soil without a living component is simply part of Earth's outer layer of loose material, described in {{ref:soil-form-097}}. More recent definitions embrace soils with no organic content at all, such as loose layers formed on Mars and in comparable deserts on Earth. Engineers sidestep the question. For them, soil is simply part of the loose material above solid rock, found also on the Moon and other celestial bodies. The sources still disagree on whether lifeless material, such as the surface material of the Moon or Mars, should be called soil.

openers.found: Most of what people grow and build rests on soil, a natural mixture of minerals, the remains of living things, gases, water and organisms. All of it together forms the pedosphere, the outermost layer of Earth's crust, where soil forms and wears away. Soil science studies this layer as a natural resource, from how it forms to how it should be used and managed. A turning point came when Dokuchaev argued that soil is a natural body with its own history, distinct from the solid rock beneath it. This first part lays the foundations on which the rest of the course builds.
openers.what-soil-is: Soil is a mixture of solid particles and pore space, with water and air sharing the pores. This chapter starts from that mixture and widens out to the layer of Earth's crust that soil makes up. It meets the science that studies soil and the two branches that grew from it, one asking how soils form and the other how they affect living things. It then turns to the many ways people rely on soil, and to how anyone can judge whether a soil is doing its jobs well.

reviews.what-soil-is: Soil is a three-state system of solids, water and gas, and about half of a typical soil is pore space. Since Dokuchaev it has been studied as a natural body with its own history, formed in the pedosphere where rock, air, water and life meet. Pedology reads that history, while edaphology asks what soil does for plants and people, from producing 98.8% of human food to filtering groundwater. Climate steers the outcome: forest soils leach into contrasting layers, dry soils pile up calcium, and tropical soils weather to rusty red. Soil health and soil quality measure how well a soil keeps doing its jobs, and even where soil ends is still debated.
